styles.name: Layered Architecture
styles.description: Organises components into horizontal layers (presentation, business logic, data access). Each layer only communicates with the layer directly below it.
strengths: Simple and well-understood pattern
Clear separation of concerns
Easy to develop and test each layer independently
Good for teams familiar with traditional n-tier architecture
weaknesses: Changes in lower layers can ripple upward
Performance overhead from passing through multiple layers
tradeoffs: Simplicity vs scalability — suitable for moderate load, not high-concurrency systems
Maintainability gains come at the cost of deployment flexibility

styles.name: MVC
styles.description: Separates application into Model (data), View (UI), and Controller (logic). Commonly used in web and desktop applications.
strengths: Clean separation of UI, logic, and data
Promotes parallel development of UI and backend
Widely supported by frameworks (Django, Spring MVC, ASP.NET)
Highly maintainable for UI-driven applications
weaknesses: Not designed for distributed or high-scale systems
Controller can become a bottleneck (fat controller anti-pattern)
Tight coupling between View and Controller in some implementations
tradeoffs: Excellent for developer productivity and maintainability, poor for scalability
Best suited for user-facing web applications with moderate traffic

styles.name: Modular Monolith
styles.description: A single deployable unit structured into well-defined internal modules with explicit boundaries and interfaces.
strengths: High internal cohesion with clear module boundaries
Easier to refactor towards microservices if needed
Simpler operational model than microservices
Low latency — no inter-service network calls
weaknesses: Still deployed as a single unit — one failure can affect all modules
Harder to scale individual modules independently
Risk of modules becoming tightly coupled over time
tradeoffs: Best balance of maintainability and simplicity for small-to-medium teams
Scalability is limited compared to microservices

styles.name: Microservices
styles.description: Decomposes the system into small, independently deployable services each responsible for a specific business capability.
strengths: Independent scaling per service
Fault isolation — failure of one service does not bring down others
Technology flexibility per service
Supports continuous deployment and independent releases
weaknesses: High operational complexity (service discovery, distributed tracing, orchestration)
Data consistency challenges across service boundaries
Requires mature DevOps and monitoring practices
tradeoffs: Exceptional scalability and availability at the cost of significant operational overhead
Suitable for large teams and high-traffic systems, not for early-stage or small projects

styles.name: Event-Driven Architecture
styles.description: Components communicate by producing and consuming events via a message broker. Services are decoupled through asynchronous event streams.
strengths: High decoupling between producers and consumers
Excellent scalability through asynchronous processing
Resilient to partial failures — events can be retried or replayed
Supports real-time and reactive workloads
weaknesses: Difficult to trace and debug event flows
Eventual consistency can be hard to reason about
Higher complexity in event schema management
Requires a reliable message broker infrastructure
tradeoffs: Strong scalability and reliability at the cost of debugging complexity
Best for systems with high-volume, asynchronous, or real-time data flows
